Q: Why the difference in handling unbound locals in functions versus classes? A:

As explained in Python FAQ - Why am I getting an UnboundLocalError?

... because when you make an assignment to a variable in a scope, that variable becomes local to that scope and shadows any similarly named variable in the outer scope. Since the last statement in foo assigns a new value to x, the compiler recognizes it as a local variable.

Consequently when earlier attempting to access the uninitialized local variable an error results.

This explains why this:

x = 10
def foo():
    x = x+1  # raises UnboundLocalError
foo()

raises an Exception, but not this:

x = 10
def faa():
    y = x+1  # x stays in global scope, since it is not assigned in local
faa()

For the class foo() it's the same, since python allows assignments of attributes to objects to any given time. The class-code assigns x as new attribute of the object a.

x = 10
class foo():
    x = x+1  # scope of x: class
a = foo()  # x = 10; a.x = foo.x = 11

is the same as:

x = 10
class foo():
    def __init__(self):
        self.x = x+1  # scope of x: instance
a = foo()  # x = 10; a.x = 11

where obviously self.x is assigned instead of x, therefore also staying in global scope. (see also here)

Q: Javascript ignore linebreaks from textarea string A:

According to the HTML standard, line breaks in a <textarea> element consist only of line feeds (\n), without carriage returns (\r). The following snippet demonstrates that carriage returns are immediately removed.

t.value = "A\r\nB";
console.log(JSON.stringify(t.value));
<textarea id="t"></textarea>

Your regular expression statement should therefore be changed to

ListNotes = ListNotes.replace(/\n/g, '<br />')

because

  • The \r will not occur (and if it did, it would come before the \n)
  • The replace method does not change the variable ListNotes, it returns the result of the replacement which you must assign to ListNotes again.

(This last bullet point is what made your attempt fail.)

Q: Is a plain write inside a synchronized block sufficient for eventual visibility to getOpaque()? A:

Does performing a plain write inside a synchronized block provide the same eventual visibility guarantees to another thread calling getOpaque() as an explicit setOpaque()?

No, being inside a synchronized block has no implications at all. A synchronized block only establishes visibility guarantees regarding another synchronized block or method using the same object for synchronization. Then, and only then, you have the guaranty that a thread entering a synchronized block or method will see the (ordinary) writes performed by the thread previously leaving a synchronized block or method.

You may see a synchronized block as having an implicit lock action at the begin and unlock action at block exit and only the synchronization order of the lock and unlock actions matters for visibility guarantees.

Is a "random" synchronized block around the write sufficient to ensure eventual visibility to an opaque read?

As said above, the guarantees are about a thread using the same object for synchronization. A “random synchronized block” therefore establishes nothing. If the JVM can prove that there is no thread potentially synchronizing on the same object, it may even eliminate all effects of the synchronization, which is a an actual thing:

The server compiler might eliminate synchronization blocks (lock elision) if it determines that an object is thread local. For example, methods of classes such as StringBuffer and Vector are synchronized because they can be accessed by different threads. However, in most scenarios, they are used in a thread local manner. In cases where the usage is thread local, the compiler might optimize and remove the synchronization blocks.

Another real life optimization that eliminates the effects of a synchronized block is lock coarsening. The JVM may merge adjacent or nested synchronized blocks when they provenly lock on the same object, only keeping the effects of the outermost block or the begin of the first and end of the last. This still results in consistent behavior, as no other thread can acquire the same lock in-between the retained lock and unlock actions anyway.

Is this behavior guaranteed by the Java Memory Model / VarHandle specification, or is it merely an implementation detail that happens to work on current JDKs?

Neither. Even in a scenario where the JVM’s code generator enforces writes of the variable at the exit of the synchronized block, there is no guaranty that your opaque read is subsequent to that point. In practice, the mechanisms used to enforce that the read is subsequent to the exit of the synchronized block are usually also sufficient to ensure visibility on their own. So, seeing that it does the intended thing is no proof that it did so because of the constructs you used in the code. It’s more likely an artifact of your testing scenario.

Can this pattern be relied upon in future JDK versions, or are we effectively "getting lucky" today?

With the information above, it should be clear that the answer is no, you can’t rely on your pattern. As documented, eliminating obsolete locks is a thing for purely local objects already. Future JVMs might be more aggressive, eliminating effects for the non-local objects too, when it can be shown that other threads won’t synchronize on that object in the future.

Further, your current test scenario does not include the knowledge of whether there is some other construct currently ensuring that the read is subsequent to the write in synchronization order (in which case you don’t know whether it will be still present in the future) or whether your tests only produces the intended result by chance.

By the way, it’s not clear why you don’t use the straight-forward way of pairing the opaque read with an opaque write. You could either change the updateSize to always use an opaque write, or add a special updateSizeOpaque method if you do not need the visibility for every update. In either case, it does not bear the overhead of volatile access.

Q: How do I find a running container by name? A:

There's a helpful post at the Docker Community Forums that shows the following "Docker only" way:

For a container named foo:

docker ps -a --no-trunc --filter name=^/foo$

Which makes another answer to your question:

docker ps --filter name=^/X$

Q: Can admin create files manually within C:\inetpub\wwwroot under Windows 8.1? A:

10 years later and I've had a similar issue on my WinServer16 VM for a college project. While I was able to create a file by logging into the Domain Administrator account, I wanted to work out how it would be done in real-world where the domain-administrator account is not used lightly. I was able to run Notepad as Administrator and then saved the test text doc to wwwroot file as intended.

I'd be interested to hear if people consider this an acceptable solution or simply a hack that shouldn't be used.

Q: How to add custom app icon to my Electron app with Electron-Vite A:

I suspect this is due to the Windows Explorer icon cache. In that case:

  • If you run the file, the correct icon would still show up in the Task Manager and Taskbar

  • If you reboot, the correct icon will likely show up in your explorer (you could also refresh icon cache)

Extra tip: You can also check the icon of the executable using 7zip:

  • Open the executable as archive with 7zip

  • Go to .rsrc/1033/ICON, your icon(s) should be there
